item.title: Constant query LCCs over the reals
item.description: arXiv:2611.13281v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: This note describes a new construction, found by ChatGPT Astra, of constant query Locally Correctable Codes (LCCs) over the real numbers. Prior constructions of constant query LCCs were exclusive to fields of positive characteristic and were conjectured not to exist over the reals. The construction uses low degree polynomial evaluations over an integer grid, together with a novel sampling procedure which outputs, for a given grid point $P$, a random quadratic curve through $P$ which intersects the grid in many other points (the decoding queries). The sampler is `smooth' in the sense that no grid point is queried with high probability. These codes have the additional property that the queried locations (the curve/grid intersections) are all nearby grid points.
item.dc:creator: Zeev Dvir

item.title: Local Modifications of Nearest-Neighbor and Min-Plus Representations
item.description: arXiv:2611.13787v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: We study how changing a Boolean-valued function at $d$ inputs affects the size and precision of its exact representations. Starting from a representation of size $m$, we prove four bounds, two for nearest-neighbor (NN) representations and two for integer min-plus representations. (i) For NN representations on a finite subset of $\mathbb{R}^n$ with $n\ge2$, at most $m+2d$ anchors suffice. The coefficient $2$ is optimal: on a three-point domain, changing one value can increase the minimum number of anchors from one to three. (ii) For NN representations on the Boolean cube with rational anchors, let $R$ be the maximum original coordinate bit length, and let $\Delta$ be the maximum bit length of the least common denominator of any one original anchor's coordinates. We construct a representation with at most $m+3d$ anchors on a common dyadic grid and coordinate bit length $O(R+\Delta+\log(n+1))$. (iii) For integer min-plus representations on the Boolean cube, we give a construction that keeps the original $m$ forms and their labels and adds at most $d$ new forms. Its maximum weight is at most $W+2n$, where $W$ is the largest absolute original coefficient, including constant terms. (iv) For integer min-plus representations on a finite rational domain $X\subset\mathbb{Q}^n$, at most $m+2d$ forms suffice. Their maximum weight is polynomially bounded in $m,d,W,n,|X|$, the coordinate bound, and the common denominator of $X$. The coefficient $2$ is again optimal: on a three-point domain, changing one value can increase the minimum number of forms from one to three. These bounds imply stability under polynomially many changes on the cube for polynomial-size representations, including those with polynomially bounded NN coordinate bit length or min-plus weight.
item.dc:creator: Liliia Redina

item.title: Feedback Vertex Set, Max Cut, and Edge Coloring on the Strong Product of a Graph and a Path
item.description: arXiv:2611.13917v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: We examine the computational complexity of well-known problems on subgraphs of the strong product of two paths. Namely, for Max Cut we show NP-hardness on induced subgraphs of $P \boxtimes P$ answering a question by Dvo\v{r}\'ak, Huynh, Joret, Liu, and Wood (2021). For 3-Edge Coloring we show NP-hardness on subgraphs of $P \boxtimes P$ and that it is equivalent to 3-Edge Coloring on planar graphs for induced subgraphs of $P \boxtimes P$. It is a long standing open question whether 3-Edge Coloring on planar graphs is NP-hard. As a second contribution, we consider graphs of the form $G \boxtimes P$ and show that Feedback Vertex Set on these graphs is FPT in the clique-width of $G$. Furthermore, we show that it can be solved in polynomial time if $G$ is chordal or co-comparable and that the computational complexity depends on the parity of $P$ if $G$ is bipartite. Namely, it is solvable in polynomial time if $P$ has an even number of vertices but is NP-complete otherwise. For Max Cut, we show that it can be solved in polynomial time if $G$ is bipartite.
item.dc:creator: Jan Diester, Kolja K\"uhn, Manuel Rapp, Samuel Schneider, Torsten Ueckerdt

item.title: The Monophonic Directed Convexities
item.description: arXiv:2611.14191v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Graph Convexity is a topic with many papers in the literature, especially on the $P_3$, geodesic, and monophonic convexities in undirected graphs. Regarding directed graphs, Erd{\H o}s et al. in 1972 and Chartrand and Zhang in 2000 obtained the first results on the $P_3$ and geodesic convexities for directed graphs, respectively. In this paper, we start the investigation of monophonic convexity on directed graphs. We define two convexities, the monophonic and the strong monophonic directed convexities, related to the minimal and the induced directed paths, respectively. We show that deciding whether a set is convex is polynomial-time solvable in the monophonic convexity, but coNP-complete in the strong monophonic convexity. For both convexities, we prove that the hull number is NP-complete even in DAGs. Regarding the monophonic convexity, we prove that the hull number is polynomial time solvable in tournaments, but the interval number is NP-complete in tournaments and also in bipartite oriented graphs.
item.dc:creator: J\'ulio Ara\'ujo, Ana Karolinna Maia, Thiago Marcilon, Nicolas Nisse, Rudini M. Sampaio

item.title: $\mathsf{SVP}_\infty$ Is NP-Hard for Power-of-two Cyclotomic Ideals
item.description: arXiv:2611.14334v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: We prove that exact decision-$\mathsf{SVP}$ in the coefficient $\ell_\infty$-norm is $\mathsf{NP}$-complete for principal ideals and free modules of rank two over the cyclotomic rings $R_n=\mathbb{Z}[X]/(X^n+1)$, where $n$ ranges over powers of two. For each case, we give a deterministic polynomial-time many-one reduction from the Subset Sum problem. For an instance with $s$ positive input integers, the output lattice has dimension $O(s)$. A solution to the original Subset Sum instance can be recovered in polynomial time from any nonzero output lattice vector of norm at most the specified bound. We also transfer these reductions from $R_n$ to the power-of-two cyclic rings $S_{2n}=\mathbb{Z}[X]/(X^{2n}-1)$. This gives $\mathsf{NP}$-completeness of decision-$\mathsf{SVP}$ in the coefficient $\ell_\infty$-norm for principal ideals and free modules of any fixed positive rank over these rings.
item.dc:creator: Yansong Feng, Jiaqi Liu, Hengyi Luo, Yanbin Pan

item.title: Complexity of Deciding Existence of Maltsev Polymorphisms of Finite Relational Structures
item.description: arXiv:2611.14379v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: In this article, we show that the problem of deciding whether a finite relational structure $\mathbf{A}$ admits a Maltsev polymorphism is a computational problem, which can be solved in polynomial time. We provide a proof of this result by reducing the problem to deciding whether a binary relational structure, associated with $\mathbf{A}$ admits such a polymorphism. In our construction of such an algorithm, we make an extensive use of a property of binary relations, which is implied by the existence of a Maltsev polymorphism, the so-called rectangularity property.
item.dc:creator: Dejan Delic, Ali Syed

item.title: Uniform Quantum Average-Case Fine-Grained Hardness of Arithmetized $k$-Orthogonal Vectors
item.description: arXiv:2611.14411v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: We study exact evaluation of the arithmetized $k$-Orthogonal Vectors polynomial $FOV^k$ of Ball et al. (2017, 2018). For every fixed integer $k \geq 3$, set $d(n) = \left \lceil \log^2 n \right \rceil$. Assuming the basic decision version of Quantum Strong Exponential-Time Hypothesis (QSETH), for every constant $\varepsilon > 0$, no uniform quantum algorithm runs in $O(n^{k/2 - \varepsilon})$ time on every input and evaluates this polynomial correctly with probability at least $3 / 4$ over a uniformly random input in $\mathbb F_{p(n)}^{knd(n)}$ and the algorithm's internal randomness, for all sufficiently large $n$. This holds when $p(n)$ is the smallest prime greater than $n^{k - 1}$ and when it is the smallest prime greater than $n^k$. Our direct reduction combines classical polynomial self-correction with calls to a quantum average-case evaluator. For the smaller prime, random sampling finds an orthogonal tuple with constant probability whenever the count is large enough to wrap around modulo $p(n)$; otherwise, the exact residue determines the answer. For the larger prime, quantum minimum finding and an asymptotic prime-gap bound account for the cost of generating the prescribed field. In view of prior isolation-based reductions permitting small characteristics, we present these results as explicit reductions for the two canonical-prime families, with all setup costs included in the uniform quantum running time. The hardness guarantee concerns single-instance exact evaluation; a matching quantum evaluation algorithm and a quantum proof-of-work protocol remain open.
item.dc:creator: Dhruv Prasad Deshpande, Abhishek Mishra

item.title: Solomonoff Induction with Reflective Oracles
item.description: arXiv:2611.14454v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: We study predictive properties of a reflective variant of Solomonoff induction formulated using reflective oracles (Fallenstein et al. 2015, Wyeth et al. 2025). We show that the resulting optimal predictor succeeds against computable predictive strategies that specify only part of the data-generating process. The argument relies on the fact that hypotheses computable from the predictor's own conditional probabilities remain within the reflective hypothesis class. In particular, the predictor learns incomplete models specified by computable interval restrictions on next-bit probabilities. We also establish weighted forms of unbiasedness and calibration. Finally, we discuss whether an optimal predictor's conditional probabilities suffice to compute every hypothesis in the reflective class.
item.dc:creator: Damini Kusum

item.title: 51 Additions per Recursive Step for Rank-23 $3\times3$ Matrix Multiplication, Machine-Checked over Arbitrary Rings
item.description: arXiv:2611.12907v1 Announce Type: cross Abstract: We present a rank-23 bilinear scheme for $3\times3$ matrix multiplication that uses 51 additions per recursive step in the alternative-basis (Karstadt-Schwartz) cost model, one below Nielsen's 52 (arXiv:2609.06588). The count 51 itself was first posted, on a different scheme, by Stapleton and Perminov (arXiv:2609.32388), found by heuristic sparse-basis search; the present work is independent and complementary: exactness and breadth rather than a single construction. The scheme is valid over every ring, so it recurses on block matrices, and its correctness is machine-checked in Lean 4/Mathlib. The count is exactly optimal for the scheme's equivalence class: we introduce an exact free-basis minimization procedure whose negative answers are exhaustion proofs, and use it to show that 51 is the minimum for this class, that 52 is exactly optimal both for Nielsen's class and for the class of the current flat-model record, and to sweep the complete Heule-Kauers-Seidl database of rank-23 classes. The sweep is complete: exactly four classes attain 51, all in a single HKS invariant family. We machine-check Stapleton and Perminov's scheme as well, and prove in Lean that their 51 is optimal for its class. Separately, we document a systematic gap between $\mathbb{F}_2$ and signed optima: the $\mathbb{F}_2$-optimal chains of a class typically admit no sign assignment under most of the class's integer sign models, and certificate lifting fails where a direct signed search succeeds.
item.dc:creator: Greg Sidebottom

item.title: A Fast Algorithm for Subspace Convolution
item.description: arXiv:2611.13134v1 Announce Type: cross Abstract: A cornerstone result in Boolean lattice theory is the subset-zeta transform, which computes the $f$-weighted subset summation problem $(Z f)(B)=\sum_{A\subseteq B}f(A)$ for all $ B\subseteq[n]$ in $O(N \log N)$ additions instead of the na\"ive $O(3^n) = O(N^{\log_2 3})$, where $N=2^n$. This paper studies the algebraic analogue of this problem--the subspace summation problem--where subsets are replaced by linear subspaces in $\mathbb{F}_q^n$. Surprisingly, we show that this problem admits a similar $\Theta_q(N_q \log N_q)$-time algorithm, where $N_q$ is the number of subspaces. This improves substantially (in both theory and practice) over lattice-based algorithms ([BHK+16, KKW16]), which are known to be optimal for addition-only algorithms over $\mathbb R$. We prove similar runtimes for inversion, rank-constrained sums and span convolution. We describe two main applications: Fast linear algebra on Grassmann graphs: Matrix--vector multiplication for arbitrary distance-invariant kernels on $N$-vertex Grassmann graphs in $O_q(N\log N)$ arithmetic operations, together with fast spectral projections and exact solutions of the corresponding linear systems. Graph coloring of low binary cut-rank graphs: An $n^{2^{r^2/4+O(1)}}$-time algorithm for computing the chromatic number and chromatic polynomial of an $n$-vertex graph, given a rank-decomposition of width $r$. We also give quantitative reductions from satisfiability and monotone constraint problems. Experiments show speedups in measured running time of up to $18$ over the covering-pair algorithm for the zeta transform, $190$ over Poisson summation for rank-constrained sums, and $22$ over the distance-matrix recurrence for Grassmann kernel multiplication. Lean 4 formalizations of the transform identities, arithmetic operation bounds, and graph-coloring constructions accompany the paper [PW26].
item.dc:creator: Shlomo A. Perles, Omri Weinstein

item.title: Computational Power of Clifford and Ising Quantum Computers
item.description: arXiv:2611.13347v1 Announce Type: cross Abstract: We extend the efficient classical simulation of Ising quantum computers from braidings to measurements. We investigate several different definitions of efficient Clifford quantum computation by varying the power of the circuit generator. In case the circuit generator can see the entire input, we give a detailed proof that efficient simulation of classical computation would imply the separation of complexity classes $\mathbf{P}$ and $\mathbf{PSPACE}$. If the circuit generator sees only the input length, we prove that Clifford quantum computers decide what we call affine languages.
item.dc:creator: Sawyer Dobson, Zhenghan Wang

item.title: Pair-Merge Tokenisation Is Hard to Approximate on Binary Strings and Strongly NP-Hard on Unary Datasets
item.description: arXiv:2611.13568v1 Announce Type: cross Abstract: Tokenisers such as Byte-Pair Encoding (BPE) shorten text by repeatedly merging an adjacent pair of symbols into a new one; fewer tokens mean less computation. We ask whether an efficient algorithm can choose $k$ merges that leave a string of length $n$ almost as short as possible; doing nothing is already within a factor $n$. We prove that, unless P = NP, no polynomial-time algorithm comes within a factor $c\,n/\log n$, for some constant $c>0$, already for one binary string and for BPE-style merges that replace every occurrence. The key idea is that $k$ merges form a grammar with $k$ rules: a vertex-cover gap becomes a grammar-size gap, which we amplify with relabelled copies, encode in binary and realise with explicit merges. For merges that may skip occurrences, a simple algorithm achieves $O(n/\log\log n)$, and no Karp reduction can prove hardness beyond order $n/\log n$ unless coNP $\subseteq$ NP/poly. Over a one-letter alphabet, both tokenisation problems left open by Kastreva et al. are strongly NP-complete on datasets with repeated strings.
item.dc:creator: Kundan Baliga, Aiden Xie, Aditya Byju

item.title: Parameterized Complexity and Geometric Approximation of Riesz Energy Subset Selection
item.description: arXiv:2611.13600v1 Announce Type: cross Abstract: We choose $k$ of $n$ sites to minimize Riesz $s$-energy, in which a pair at distance $t$ contributes $t^{-s}$. For $s=2$, exact selection is polynomial on a line but NP-hard in the plane. Adapting the proxy lemma of Ceccarello et al. gives an efficient parameterized approximation scheme (EPAS) for fixed Euclidean dimension and fixed $s>0$. To sharpen the bound, we start with a geometric packing. Farthest-first traversal gives $2k$ centers separated by at least the last insertion distance $r$. If one site of an optimum is removed, each of the $k-1$ remaining sites excludes at most one center closer than $r/2$, leaving at least $k+1$ centers free. The new step is a discrete exchange bound: the removed site's interaction energy is at most the average it would contribute at those free centers. In the plane at $s=2$, this reduces the representative bound from $O(k^2\log(2k)/\varepsilon^2)$ for a packing estimate of total energy to $O(k\log(2k)/\varepsilon^2)$, independently of $n$. Rational planar examples show that the resulting separation scale $r/\sqrt{\log(2k)}$ is sharp. A $(1+\varepsilon)$ approximation on rational planar sites takes $O(nk+n\log n)+(C\log(2k)/\varepsilon^2)^k$ operations of polynomial bit cost. The observed number $M$ of representatives determines the search size $\binom{M}{k}$. With one million sites, $k=5$ and $\varepsilon=1/2$, the exchange grid left 252 subsets on clustered inputs and about $9.3\times10^{26}$ on uniform inputs. The method extends to metrics of bounded doubling dimension and to compact domains with effective geometric routines, including filled simple polygons. At $s=2$, exact decision on metrics with nonzero distances in $\{1,2\}$ is W[1]-complete in $k$. A gap that shrinks with $k$ rules out a deterministic EPAS on unrestricted metrics unless FPT = W[1].
item.dc:creator: Michael Emmerich (Faculty of Information Technology, University of Jyv\"askyl\"a, Finland), Soumen Atta (Faculty of Information Technology, University of Jyv\"askyl\"a, Finland)

item.title: From Worst-Case to Smoothed Complexity in Continuous Optimization
item.description: arXiv:2611.14282v1 Announce Type: cross Abstract: Worst-case complexity bounds often fail to reflect the practical performance of optimization algorithms, while average-case complexity heavily relies on the distribution of the input. In this work, we develop a smoothed-analysis framework for classical continuous optimization algorithms by studying their behaviour on random perturbations of arbitrary functions. Our main contribution is to apply methods suited for non-degenerate functions to perturbations of degenerate functions, thereby recovering the faster best-known rates for the non-degenerate class. We derive smoothed complexity guarantees for several standard methods, including (Accelerated) Gradient Descent, Conjugate Gradient, and Newton-type methods, under various settings including nonconvex ones, and show that these bounds can substantially improve upon their worst-case guarantees, bringing them closer to the practical behaviour of the respective methods.
item.dc:creator: Daniel Cortild, Coralia Cartis

item.title: The Exact Complexity of Majority in Depth-Three Circuits with Bottom Fan-in Three
item.description: arXiv:2601.04072v3 Announce Type: replace Abstract: Lecomte and Ramakrishnan (arXiv'26) recently presented a depth-three circuit of size $2^{O(\sqrt{n})}$ that computes the Majority function, refuting a long held conjecture. Nevertheless, as a fundamental computational primitive which ubiquitously appears across computer science, determining the exact complexity of Majority down to the constant in the exponent, remains important. Gurumukhani et al. (CCC'24) initiated the study of optimal $\Sigma^k_3$ circuits computing the Majority function. In this work, we determine the exact $\Sigma^3_3$ complexity of Majority up to polynomial factors. We show that for any $t \le n/2$, given an $n$-variate $t$-threshold 3-CNF, i.e., with no satisfying assignment with Hamming weight less than $t$, the number of weight-$t$ satisfying assignments is at most $2^t(3/2)^{(n-t)/2}$. Along with a matching construction for $t = n/2$, the result implies that the size of the smallest $\Sigma^3_3$ circuit computing Majority is exactly $poly(n)(2/6^{1/4})^n$. The proof involves two main ingredients: - Reduction to monotone: We formulate a linear program (LP) which is defined only with respect to the monotone part of the formula. We show that bounding the cost function of this LP implies our desired upper bound on the number of minimum weight solutions of the general formula. - Structure of extremal formulas: To bound the cost function of the LP, we develop an extensive inductive argument. The inductive steps are determined by a close inspection of the local structure of extremal formulas with respect to minimum weight. Our result has a natural hypergraph interpretation: it bounds the number of independent sets of size $n-t$ under the condition that the independence number is $n-t$. This is a generalized hypergraph Tur\'an problem and coincides with the classical hypergraph Tur\'an problem at threshold $t=n-k$ for $k$-uniform hypergraphs.
item.dc:creator: Mohit Gurumukhani, Daniel Kleber, Ramamohan Paturi, Christopher Rosin, Michael Saks, Navid Talebanfard

item.title: SVP Is NP-Hard for Some Rank-2 Cyclotomic Modules
item.description: arXiv:2609.01469v2 Announce Type: replace Abstract: Let $q$ be an odd prime. Let $\zeta_q$ be a primitive $q$th root of unity, and put $K=\mathbb{Q}(\zeta_q)$, with ring of integers $\mathcal{O}_K=\mathbb{Z}[\zeta_q]$. As $q$ ranges over odd primes, we prove that the decision version of the Shortest Vector Problem ($\mathsf{SVP}$) in the canonical $\ell_2$-norm is $\mathsf{NP}$-complete on full-rank free submodules of $\mathcal{O}_K^2$ by giving a deterministic polynomial-time many-one reduction from Exact Cover by 3-Sets (X3C). The module rank is fixed at two. The main obstacle is closure under the action of $\mathcal{O}_K$. A module containing a nonzero vector also contains every scalar multiple of that vector by a nonzero element of $\mathcal{O}_K$, and some of these multiples may be shorter. Three ideas overcome this obstacle. First, we map the Bennett--Peikert Reed--Solomon lattice to a principal cyclotomic ideal and use Wan's point-count estimates to prove that a coset of this ideal contains many binary coefficient representatives. Second, we construct a checker whose canonical squared norm encodes the X3C equations, with a controlled nonnegative error term. Third, the checker and a second module coordinate combine with a separation bound for ideal cosets to rule out short vectors in NO instances. Each constructed instance consists of an odd prime $q$, two integral generators whose $2\times2$ generator matrix has nonzero determinant, and an integer squared threshold. The construction also gives $\mathsf{NP}$-hardness of search-$\mathsf{SVP}$ under deterministic polynomial-time Turing reductions with at most one oracle call.
item.dc:creator: Jiaqi Liu, Yansong Feng, Yanbin Pan

item.title: On derandomizing the line-point low-degree test
item.description: arXiv:2611.09183v2 Announce Type: replace Abstract: We investigate the derandomized version of the classical line-point low-degree test in the high-error regime in the bivariate setting and reveal some unexpected behavior. The classical line-point low-degree test takes an $m$-variate function $f$ over a finite field $\mathbb{F}_q$, queries it along a random line and accepts if the restriction of the function to this line is a low-degree polynomial. The high-error version of (the analysis of) this test asserts that if $f$ has at least $\epsilon$ expected local agreement with a degree-$k$ univariate polynomial on a random line, then in fact $f$ is non-trivially close to some degree-$k$ $m$-variate polynomial even as $\epsilon$ approaches $0$ (provided $q$ is sufficiently large compared to $k$ and $1/\epsilon$). The derandomized version of the problem asks if the same holds when the line is not chosen uniformly over all possible lines but rather from a small set. In this paper we explore the bivariate case ($m=2$). We show, somewhat surprisingly, that there exists a function $f\colon \mathbb{F}_q^2 \to \mathbb{F}_q$ and a set of lines $\mathcal{L}$ in $\mathbb{F}_q^2$ of size nearly $q^{3/2}$ such that on every line in $\mathcal{L}$, $f$ has agreement $\approx 1/2$ on average with some univariate polynomial of degree $k=\sqrt{q}/2$ and yet $f$ is $1 - O(q^{-1/2})$ far from every polynomial of degree $O(k)$. On the positive side, we show that once the field size $q$ is at least $k^2/(\epsilon)^{O(1)}$ such examples disappear and we can get sets of lines of size $O(q/\epsilon^{O(1)})$ on which the low-degree test has a high-error analysis. On the way to our positive result, we show a new high-degree version of the classical two-direction Polishchuk--Spielman divisibility lemma.
item.dc:creator: Prahladh Harsha, Swastik Kopparty, Mrinal Kumar, Ramprasad Saptharishi, Madhu Sudan

item.title: Computational complexity of Berry phase estimation in topological phases of matter
item.description: arXiv:2509.13423v4 Announce Type: replace-cross Abstract: The Berry phase is a fundamental quantity in the classification of topological phases of matter. In this paper, we present a new quantum algorithm and several complexity-theoretical results for the Berry phase estimation (BPE) problems. Our new quantum algorithm achieves BPE in a more general setting than previously known quantum algorithms, with a theoretical guarantee. For the complexity-theoretic results, we consider two main cases. First, we prove $\mathsf{BQP}$-completeness when we are given a guiding state that has a large overlap with the ground state. This result establishes an exponential quantum speedup for estimating the Berry phase. Second, we prove $\mathsf{UQMA} \cap \mathsf{co}$-$\mathsf{UQMA}$-completeness when we have an $\textit{a priori}$ bound for the ground-state energy. Here, $\mathsf{UQMA}$ is the unique witness version of $\mathsf{QMA}$, and $\mathsf{UQMA} \cap \mathsf{co}$-$\mathsf{UQMA}$ precisely captures the complexity of BPE without the known guiding state. Remarkably, this problem is, to our knowledge, the first natural problem complete for $\mathsf{UQMA} \cap \mathsf{co}$-$\mathsf{UQMA}$. These results advance the role of quantum computing in the study of topological phases of matter and provide a pathway for clarifying the connection between topological phases of matter and computational complexity.
item.dc:creator: Ryu Hayakawa, Kazuki Sakamoto, Chusei Kiumi

item.title: Differentially Private Verification of Distribution Properties
item.description: arXiv:2604.10819v3 Announce Type: replace-cross Abstract: A recent line of work initiated by Chiesa and Gur and further developed by Herman and Rothblum investigates the sample and communication complexity of verifying properties of distributions with the assistance of a powerful, knowledgeable, but untrusted prover. In this work, we initiate the study of differentially private distribution property verification. After all, if we do not trust the prover to help us with verification, why should we trust it with our sensitive sample? We map a landscape of differentially private verification of properties of distributions. In the non-private case it is known that one-round private-coin protocols can have substantially lower complexity than public-coin (AM) protocols. In contrast, the possibility for improvement in differentially private interactive proofs depends on the privacy parameter regime and model. Drawing on connections between privacy and replicability and privacy amplification techniques in the literature we show: 1. There exists a reduction from any one-round $(\varepsilon,\delta)$-differentially private private-coin protocol to a differentially private AM protocol for the parameter regime $\varepsilon = O(1/\sqrt{s})$ and $\delta= O(1/s^{5/2})$ with approximately the same privacy and sample and communication complexities. In the local model, this is relaxed to $\varepsilon = O(1/\sqrt{\log s})$ 2. However, when the privacy guarantee is very relaxed ($\varepsilon \in \Omega(\log s)$), private coins indeed reduce sample and communication complexities. We also obtain a computationally efficient Merlin-Arthur proof for privately testing whether samples are drawn from a product distribution and prove that its sample complexity is optimal up to a $polylog N$ factor by reducing uniformity testing to independence testing with Boolean attributes and appealing to known lower bounds on sample complexity for private uniformity testing.
item.dc:creator: Elbert Du, Cynthia Dwork, Pranay Tankala, Linjun Zhang

item.title: Query Complexity of Testing Structured Parenthesis Languages
item.description: arXiv:2609.37431v2 Announce Type: replace-cross Abstract: We study the query complexity of testing membership in structured string languages, focusing on Dyck languages and natural generalizations. A tester receives query access to a word and must distinguish valid inputs from words that are far in Hamming distance, while inspecting only a sublinear number of positions. Our results sharpen the boundary between constant-query testability and polynomial query complexity. First, we prove an $\Omega(n^{2/5})$ lower bound for testing Dyck languages $D_m$ with any fixed number $m\ge2$ of parenthesis types, improving the previous $\Omega(n^{1/5})$ lower bound of Fischer, Magniez, and Starikovskaya (SODA `18) and nearly matching their upper bound of $O(n^{2/5+o(1)})$. Furthermore, we show that all nonadaptive algorithms for these problems require $\Omega(n^{1/2})$ queries. Our lower bounds use a P\'olya-urn process to construct the hard distribution; Second, we identify a broad class of weighted-parenthesis languages, which we call {\em excursion languages,} that remain constant-query testable. These languages encode bounded-step walks that stay nonnegative and return to zero. For every fixed excursion language, we give a nonadaptive tester with query complexity $O(1/\varepsilon^2)$, and we prove this dependence on $\varepsilon$ is optimal, even for adaptive algorithms. As a special case, we obtain the tight $\Theta(1/\varepsilon^2)$ query complexity of testing $D_1$, improving the previous $O(\log(1/\varepsilon)/\varepsilon^2)$ upper bound and giving the first matching two-sided-error lower bound. Third, we construct a simple hard language, Hidden String, that is generated by a deterministic linear grammar but nevertheless requires $\Omega(n^{2/5})$ adaptive queries and $\Omega(n^{1/2})$ nonadaptive queries to test. This shows that polynomial query complexity appears even for highly restricted string languages.
item.dc:creator: Tim Jackman, Diptaksho Palit, Sofya Raskhodnikova
